title: Meet the Microbe That Hulks Out and Eats Its Own Kind
summary: Imagine a tiny single-celled organism that occasionally transforms into a giant, cannibalistic version of itself. That's exactly what scientists discovered in a Caribbean aquarium filter. The microbe, named Euplotes gigatrox, is a ciliate—a type of protist covered in hairlike structures called cilia. Normally, it grazes peacefully on bacteria. But under certain conditions, a few individuals balloon to more than twice their normal size and start devouring their smaller siblings. Ben Larson, a cell biologist at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, found these "Hulked-out" microbes in gunk from an aquarium in Curaçao. The transformation happens in stages. "A cell gets a big mouth," Larson says. "Then they start running around like crazy." Once a would-be giant catches a sibling in its enlarged mouth, its entire body plan changes, and it grows into an "enormous cannibalistic supergiant." Normal-size cells walk and swim, but the giants can only walk in circles. Interestingly, the giants can revert to normal size through lopsided cell division. While a regular cell divides once per day, a shrinking giant can produce up to nine normal offspring in a single day, and up to 16 over five days. Each division makes the giant a bit smaller until it returns to normal. The researchers found that up to 42 percent of the species' genes are involved in this size shift. Understanding how a single-celled organism switches between such different behaviors could provide clues about how simple life forms develop complex traits—and perhaps how multicellular life first evolved.
why_it_matters: This microbe offers a rare window into how a single cell can reorganize itself into dramatically different forms, which is a basic question behind cell specialization and multicellular life. If scientists can identify the genetic switches involved, they may better understand how complex bodies evolved from simple ancestors.

background_read: Ciliates are a group of single-celled protists found in freshwater, soil, and marine environments; they use rows of hairlike cilia to move and sweep in food.

The species in this study was collected from an aquarium in Curaçao (a Caribbean island nation) and described by Ben Larson, a cell biologist at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (a science and engineering university in Troy, New York).

Many microbes can change shape or behavior in response to stress, hunger, or crowding, a phenomenon called phenotypic plasticity, but an individual that shifts between normal grazing and giant cannibalism is extreme.
Biologists study such switches because they may help explain how cells regulate their own size and identity.
Understanding how a single cell can produce different body plans is also a clue to how multicellular organisms, whose cells specialize into different roles, might have first evolved.
Curaçao's warm coastal waters and aquariums contain diverse microbial life, making them useful places to find unusual species.
Larson's team found that nearly half of the organism's genes are involved, suggesting the transformation is a major reorganization, not a simple reaction.

perspectives.description: Researchers who study evolution see Euplotes gigatrox as a useful model because the transformation is visible, fast, and reversible. It could reveal genetic rules for changing cell size and shape without requiring complex multicellular tissues.

Some biologists might caution that a cannibalistic aquarium microbe is an odd exception, not a direct mirror of early multicellular life. Lab conditions may trigger behavior that rarely matters in the wild, so its evolutionary meaning is uncertain.

The fact that up to 42 percent of the species' genes respond to the size shift suggests the change is a systemic reorganization rather than a single switch. Studying how a lone cell toggles between grazing and cannibalism provides a controlled way to examine plasticity.

Future work could identify the exact molecular signals that trigger transformation and reversal. Those findings might help researchers understand how cells in multicellular organisms decide to grow, divide, or specialize — and how those decisions can go wrong.
